title: Coordinate Format Detector: Name That Format
description: Identify a decimal-degree coordinate pair's format before using it with the Coordinate Format Detector — quick, local, unambiguous. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, '40.7580, -73.9855' is instantly recognisable as signed decimal degrees — while '40.7580, 73.9855' with no minus is a hemisphere question the detector helps you ask before a map misplaces you by an ocean.
quick_answer: The Coordinate Format Detector identifies a simple decimal-degree coordinate pair before you use it in mapping tools. Paste the pair and read the verdict — format, hemisphere reading and the sanity checks that catch swapped axes and missing signs before they become wrong maps.

body.t: A spreadsheet of mystery pairs gets its format named column-wise before any import — then the
PDFs and emails mangle coordinates creatively. The detector's verdict tells you what survived the journey.
The map shows the point in the sea off Africa (0,0's neighbourhood) or mirrored — format and sign problems, detectable here in one paste.
Students paste examples and defend the verdict — the fastest route to actually seeing formats instead of fearing them.

'-73.9855, 40.7580' puts longitude first. A latitude of −73.9855 is legal (southern ocean!) while 40.7580 as longitude is legal too — only the context convicts the swap, and the detector's range-and-context read is built for exactly this.
US coordinates pasted without the western minus land in Central Asia. The detector flags hemisphere plausibility for the region you expect — the cheapest bug in geospatial work, caught.

faq: Which format is detected?
Decimal-degree pairs and their close dresses — the page names the format and reads the hemispheres, ranges and likely axis order.
What about DMS, UTM and MGRS?
They announce themselves by symbols and scale (see the signature table). DMS converts on its own page; grid systems have dedicated converters — the detector points you at the right one.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
Detection is datum-blind by nature — formats exist independent of datums. The site's working datum is WGS84.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
The detector reads precision as a clue about the source (survey exports carry more places than typed notes) — a hint, never a verdict.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
The verdict tells you how to import; the Coordinate Converter then produces the exact dress your GIS wants.
It says ambiguous.
Some strings honestly are (two small positive numbers fit several readings). Ambiguity reported beats a confident wrong map — resolve with context: which continent should this be on?
Lat/lon order worldwide?
Geographic convention says lat, lon; much software says lon, lat (x, y). The detector's context read is precisely the guard between them.
Degrees with a comma decimal separator?
European documents write 40,7580 — a parser trap the detector's format read can flag before the comma splits your pair into three numbers.
Batch detection?
One string at a time here — the triage instrument. Columns of them belong to the parser plus your spreadsheet, spot-checked here.
Why not just try it on a map?
Because a wrong-format point often still lands somewhere plausible-looking. Detection before mapping is the order that catches the plausible wrongness.
Mobile GPS strings?
Phones emit signed decimals from their APIs and dressed formats in their compass apps — both are home territory for the detector and converter pair.
